title: Why I Want to Be the Most Boring Teacher in the Building
author: SoL in the Wild
summary: SoL in the Wild argues that the entertaining, high-energy "great teacher" performance that impresses classroom observers rarely produces durable learning, and now embraces being called "boring" as evidence of doing the job right. Early in their career, a loud, colourful, fast-moving classroom looked impressive but left little behind when they checked what students actually remembered days or weeks later, prompting a shift toward the science of learning (citing Willingham, Rosenshine, and Lemov). The resulting classroom runs on visible routine -- writing, retrieval, elaboration, dual coding, turn-and-talk, repeated daily -- which they argue frees working memory for actual thinking rather than emotional novelty. The piece closes with a reclamation of "boring" as a proxy for consistent, clear, and evidence-based teaching, arguing the trade of short-term applause for long-term retention is one worth making every time.
points: The central argument is a direct challenge to how "good teaching" is often judged by observers: visible engagement (energy, noise, performance) and durable long-term learning are treated as though they're the same thing, when the author's own experience suggests they're often in tension.

The piece's diagnostic test is retrospective, not observational: checking what students remembered days or weeks later, rather than how the lesson looked or felt in the moment, is what exposed the gap between an exciting classroom and an effective one.

Predictability is reframed as a cognitive resource rather than a stylistic flaw -- routine (write, retrieve, elaborate, dual code, turn and talk, every day) is argued to free up working memory specifically because it removes the need to process novelty.
The piece explicitly redefines "boring" as a proxy for three specific qualities -- consistent, clear, evidence-based -- rather than accepting it as a synonym for ineffective or low-energy teaching.
quotes: We've built this myth of the great teacher - the one who dazzles, performs, entertains. Always upbeat. Always engaging. But here's the truth the hallway observers don't see: the flash rarely sticks.

I thought fun meant effective. My classroom was loud, colorful, fast-moving. It looked impressive. But when I checked what students actually remembered days and weeks later, it was like watching a Snapchat story disappear.
Learning that lasts is built on often unpleasant friction: retrieval, reflection, feedback, and practice.
Predictability frees up working memory for actual thinking. It creates safety and rhythm. It tells students, this is a place where your brain works hard, not your emotions.
Boring means consistent. Boring means clear. Boring means evidence-based.
The one who teaches for learning over the long-term, not for applause in the short-term.
